{{short description|Constructed language}} {{multiple issues | {{primary sources | date = March 2013}} {{refimprove | date = March 2013}} {{notability | date = January 2025}} }} {{infobox language | created = 1982 | creator = [[Suzette Haden Elgin]] and collaborators | fam2 = [[artistic language|artistic]] and [[philosophical language|philosophical]] language | fam3 = [[fictional language]] | glotto = laad1235 | iso3 = ldn | name = Láadan | notice = IPA | posteriori = [[a priori language]], with influences from [[Navajo language|Navajo]] and [[English language|English]] | setting = experiment in [[feminism|feminist]] [[linguistics]], and featured in Elgin's [[novel]] series beginning with ''[[Native Tongue (Elgin novel)|Native Tongue]]'' }} '''Láadan'''{{DEFAULTSORT:Laadan}} ({{IPA|ldn|ˈlɑ˦ɑˈdɑn|audio=LL-Q35757 (ldn)-Arlo Barnes-Láadan.wav}}) is a [[gynocentrism|gynocentric]] [[constructed language]] created by [[Suzette Haden Elgin]] in 1982 to test the [[Linguistic relativity|Sapir–Whorf hypothesis]],{{cite book | date = 20 September 2016 | first1 = Joshua | first2 = Dylan | first3 = Ella | isbn = 9780761169086 | last1 = Foer | last2 = Thuras | last3 = Morton | page = 23 | publisher = Workman | title = Atlas Obscura | title-link = Atlas Obscura#Publications }} specifically to determine if development of a language aimed at expressing the views of women would shape a culture; a subsidiary hypothesis was that Western [[natural language]]s may be better suited for expressing the views of men than women. The language was included in her [[science fiction]] [[Native Tongue (Suzette Haden Elgin novel)|''Native Tongue'']] series. Láadan contains a number of words that are used to make unambiguous statements that include how one feels about what one is saying. According to Elgin, this is designed to counter [[androcentrism|male-centered]] language's limitations on women, who are forced to respond "I know I said that, but I meant this".{{huh|date=September 2025|reason=the quoted phrase out of context is ..er... ambiguous, if not outright nonsense}} == Motivation, development and publication history == Elgin was a writer of both fiction and nonfiction book series.{{cite journal | access-date = 2023-02-15 | date = 2015 | first = M. А. | issn = 2312-2919 | issue = 2 | journal = Bulletin of Dnipropetrovsk University. Series 'Linguistics' | language = uk | last = Strazheva | location = [[Dnipro]] | publisher = [[Alfred Nobel University]] | title = ИСКУССТВЕННЫЙ ЯЗЫК ЛААДАН КАК ЯЗЫКОВОЙ ЭКСПЕРИМЕНТ В ХУДОЖЕСТВЕННОМ ТЕКСТЕ | trans-title = Сonstructed Language Láadan as a Linguistic Experiment in the Literary Text | url = http://www.irbis-nbuv.gov.ua/cgi-bin/irbis_nbuv/cgiirbis_64.exe?C21COM=2&I21DBN=UJRN&P21DBN=UJRN&IMAGE_FILE_DOWNLOAD=1&Image_file_name=PDF/vdumo_2015_23_21(2)__22.pdf | volume = 21 }} Láadan and the ideas underpinning its creation were described in several series: It was included as a [[fictional language|language]] portrayed [[diegesis#Literature|diegetically]] within the [[speculative fiction]] novel trilogy ''Native Tongue'' (1984), ''The Judas Rose'' (1987), and ''Earthsong'' (1993). The role of the language in the plot of the overall story is as a transformative project, whose development changes the social roles of an extended family of linguist characters. After the publication of the second novel, ''A First Dictionary & Grammar of Láadan'' (1988) was published in the hopes that a community of speakers could form, and the validity of the project from the novels might be tested in [[real life]]. The [[grammar book]] was advertised in literary and feminist magazines, and feedback led to a second edition and posthumously a third edition. Before conceiving of Láadan, Elgin had published a [[self-help]] book ''The Gentle Art of Verbal Self Defense'' (1980) which was developed into a series of books focusing on the workplace, romantic relationships, and so on. It postulated that at least in English, phrasing often allowed for an ambiguous hostility which could be used as a sort of [[verbal abuse]] especially in competitive environments, and discussed which defenses might be effective and which not; see {{section link|verbal self-defense|Influential contributors}}. To allow for the means to express [[emotional expression#Psychological construction model|nuanced emotion]] and other distinctions, [[feature (linguistics)|feature]]s combine to create and modify meanings. == Phonology == === Tones === Láadan is a [[tone (linguistics)|tonal language]]. It utilises two distinct tones{{efn| Some people analyze these tone sequences as tonemic as well, for a total of four tones. By this analysis, the word "Láadan" would thus be considered to have two syllables, {{IPA|/lâː/}} and /dan/. Elgin preferred an analysis of the language as having no long vowels and a single tone, the high tone (distinguished from "neutral, baseline pitch"), but she acknowledged that linguists using other formalisms would be justified in saying that there are two tones, high and low (or unmarked or mid).}}: * {{lang|ldn|lo}}{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/lō/}} or {{IPA|/lò/}}, a short, medium or low tone, represented by a single unmarked vowel * {{lang|ldn|ló}}{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/ló/}}, a short, high tone, represented by a single marked vowel The word "Láadan" has three syllables: "lá-" with the short vowel /a/ plus high tone; "-a" with the short vowel /a/ and no tone; and "-dan". Láadan does not allow any double (i.e. [[Length (phonetics)|long]]) phonemes. Whenever two identical short vowels would occur side by side in a single morpheme, one of them has to be marked for high tone. When adding an affix would result in two identical vowels side by side, an [[Epenthesis|epenthetic]] /h/ is inserted to prevent the forbidden sequence. The language will allow either {{lang|ldn|máa}} or {{lang|ldn|maá}}, but not *maa. These combinations can be described as: * {{lang|ldn|loó}}{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/lǒː/}}, a long, low-rising tone, represented by a double vowel, the second of which is marked * {{lang|ldn|lóo}}{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/lôː/}}, a long, high-falling tone, represented by a double vowel, the first of which is marked === Vowels === Láadan has five [[vowel]]s: * ''a''{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/ɑ/}}, an [[open back unrounded vowel]] (as [[English language|English]] ''calm''), * ''e''{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/ɛ/}}, an [[open-mid front unrounded vowel]] (as English ''bell''), * ''i''{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/ɪ/}}, a [[near-close near-front unrounded vowel]] (as English ''bit''), * ''o''{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/o/}}, a [[close-mid back rounded vowel]] (as English ''home''), * ''u''{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/u/}}, a [[close back rounded vowel]] (as English ''boon''). === Consonants === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" ! colspan="2" rowspan="2"| ! rowspan="2"| [[Labial consonant|Labial]] ! colspan="2"| [[Dental consonant|Dental]] /

[[Lateral consonant|lateral]] |- ! colspan="2" | [[Nasal consonant|Nasal]] | m {{IPAslink|m}} | n {{IPAslink|n}} | | | |- ! colspan=2|[[Plosive]] | b {{IPAslink|b}} | d {{IPAslink|d}} | | | |- ! rowspan="2" | [[Fricative]] ! style="font-size: x-small;" | voiceless | | th {{IPAslink|θ}} | lh {{IPAslink|ɬ}} | sh {{IPAslink|ʃ}} | h {{IPAslink|h}} |- ! style="font-size: x-small;" | voiced | | | | zh {{IPAslink|ʒ}} | |- ! colspan="2" | [[Approximant]] | w {{IPAslink|w}} | r {{IPAslink|ɹ}} | l {{IPAslink|l}} | y {{IPAslink|j}} | |} Láadan lacks the [[consonant]]s {{IPA|/p, t, k, ɡ, s, z, f, v/}}. It uses ''b'', ''d'', ''sh'' ({{IPA|/ʃ/}}), ''m'', ''n'', ''l'', ''r'', ''w'', ''y'' ({{IPA|/j/}}), ''h'' with the same phonetic value as English. Three [[Digraph (orthography)|digraphs]] require further explanation: * ''th''{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/θ/}}, a [[voiceless dental fricative]] (always as in English ''think'', never as ''then''), * ''zh''{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/ʒ/}}, a [[voiced postalveolar fricative]] (as English ''plea'''s'''ure''), * ''lh''{{spaced ndash}}{{IPA|/ɬ/}}, a [[voiceless alveolar lateral fricative]] (as [[Welsh language|Welsh]] {{lang|cy|llan}}). == Grammar == === Mandatory parts of speech === Most Láadan sentences, and all formal sentences in the language, contain three [[grammatical particle|particles]]: * The ''speech-act'' particle{{spaced ndash}}this occurs at the beginning of the sentence and marks it as either a statement ({{lang|ldn|bíi}}), a question ({{lang|ldn|báa}}), ''et cetera''; in connected speech or writing, this particle is often omitted. They are: *; {{lang|ldn|Bíi}} : Indicates a declarative sentence (usually optional) *; {{lang|ldn|Báa}} : Indicates a question *; {{lang|ldn|Bó}} : Indicates a command; very rare, except to small children *; {{lang|ldn|Bóo}} : Indicates a request; this is the usual imperative/"command" form *; {{lang|ldn|Bé}} : Indicates a promise *; {{lang|ldn|Bée}} : Indicates a warning * The [[grammatical tense]] particle{{spaced ndash}}this occurs second in the sentence and marks it as either [[present tense]] ({{lang|ldn|ril}}), [[past tense]] ({{lang|ldn|eril}}), [[future tense]] ({{lang|ldn|aril}}) or hypothetical ({{lang|ldn|wil}}); without the tense particle, the sentence is assumed to have the same tense as the previous sentence. * The [[evidentiality|evidence]] particle{{spaced ndash}}this occurs at the end of statements and indicates the trustworthiness of the statement.{{efn|[[Lojban]] was developed around the same time as Láadan and was influenced to use evidentials.{{cite web|title=Oooh! Arrgh! Ugh! Yecch! Attitudinal and Emotional Indicators - The Lojban Reference Grammar|url=https://lojban.github.io/cll/13/11}}}} They are: *; {{lang|ldn|wa}} : Known to speaker because perceived by speaker, externally or internally *; {{lang|ldn|wi}} : Known to speaker because self-evident *; {{lang|ldn|we}} : Perceived by speaker in a dream *; {{lang|ldn|wáa}} : Assumed true by speaker because speaker trusts source *; {{lang|ldn|waá}} : Assumed false by speaker because speaker distrusts source; if evil intent by the source is also assumed, the form is {{lang|ldn|waálh}} *; {{lang|ldn|wo}} : Imagined or invented by speaker, hypothetical *; {{lang|ldn|wóo}} : Used to indicate that the speaker states a total lack of knowledge as to the validity of the matter === Word order === Láadan has two syntactic orderings. In [[active voice]], it is a [[verb–subject–object]] (VSO) language; the English example sentence in the following table would read in {{langx|ldn|Bíi eril {{underline|yod}} {{underline|Sham}} {{underline|doyu}}th wa}}. In [[passive voice]], it is an [[object–verb–subject]] (OVS) language; the sentence would read in {{langx|ldn|Bíi eril {{underline|doyu}}th {{underline|yod}} {{underline|Sham}}eshub wa}}. In either case, it uses a minority word order type among languages of the world. {{language word order frequency}} [[Verb]]s and [[adjective]]s are interchangeable. There are no [[article (grammar)|articles]], and the object is marked by the {{lang|ldn|-th}} or {{lang|ldn|-eth}} [[suffix]]. The [[plural]] number is shown only by the {{lang|ldn|me-}} prefix to the verb. The particle {{lang|ldn|ra}} following a verb makes it negative. Separate clauses are joined by the particle {{lang|ldn|hé}}.

{{lang|ldn|thulid}}: "father" |} The ''speech-act'' particle, at the beginning of a sentence, can also carry several suffixes, which expand on the overall state of the sentence. For example, {{lang|ldn|bíi}} begins a statement, but {{lang|ldn|bíide}} begins a statement that is part of a narrative; {{lang|ldn|bóoth}} begins a request made in pain; {{lang|ldn|báada}} begins a question that is meant in jest. === Pronouns === [[Pronoun]]s in Láadan are built up from a number of constituent parts. The consonant ''l'' marks the [[grammatical person|first person]], ''n'' the second person and ''b'' the third person. Usually, these are followed by the vowel ''e''. The vowel ''a'' is used to designate someone who is loved ({{lang|ldn|lhe-}} is prefixed to describe someone who is despised). The suffix {{lang|ldn|-zh}} is used to mark a plural pronoun for numbers up to four, and {{lang|ldn|-n}} for numbers beyond that. Therefore, {{lang|ldn|lazh}} means "we, several beloved", and {{lang|ldn|lheben}} means "they, many despised". == Reception == [[Anthony Burgess]] mentioned Láadan in a 1985 review of ''[[A Feminist Dictionary]]'' in ''[[The Observer]]'', calling it "ingenious" and stating he was "highly sympathetic" of its aims, but asserting that "it's not going to work" because "[n]ot enough women care sufficiently".{{cite news|title=Penile Servitude|url=https://newspapers.com/article/the-observer-penile-servitude/181287588|page=26|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|newspaper=[[The Observer]]}} Burgess had experience with [[fictional language]]s from developing the [[Nadsat]] argot for his 1962 novel ''[[A Clockwork Orange (novel)|A Clockwork Orange]]''. == See also == * [[Language and gender]] * [[Muted group theory]] == Notes == {{notelist}} == References == {{reflist}} == Further reading == *Elgin, Suzette Haden, & Diane Martin.
